extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (agents/attorneys) and USPTO disciplinary personnel/adjudicators
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural criteria used in USPTO disciplinary proceedings against practitioners (service, answering complaints, rules-of-conduct violations, burdens of proof, and factors for determining sanctions). Applies to evaluating practitioner misconduct and selecting appropriate discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.103 — diligence and promptness
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations include failing to pay required filing fees, failing to respond to Notices to File Missing Parts, failing to file required documents (e.g., Application Data Sheet, oath/declaration), failing to timely file applications claimed by the client, failing to obtain or correctly file client signatures on power of attorney forms, and otherwise allowing client matters to be abandoned. The decision lists numerous specific failures as examples of breaching § 11.103.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(2) — reasonable consultation about means
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall reasonably consult with the client about the means by which the client’s objectives are to be accomplished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to consult about material decisions (e.g., filing without claiming priority) constitutes a violation. The decision finds Respondent violated this rule by failing to consult Inventors about filing the application without a priority claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3) — keep client reasonably informed
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of violation include not notifying clients of Notices to File Missing Parts, failure to update clients after repeated requests, not returning calls, and not informing clients of abandonment or other critical Office communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(b) — explain matters for informed decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall explain a matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations include failing to explain the substance of Office notices (e.g., Notice to File Missing Parts, Notice Regarding Power of Attorney, Notice of Abandonment), failing to explain consequences (that an application would be filed on a given date, or become abandoned), and failing to provide necessary status information to allow informed client choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.116(a)(3) — withdrawal when discharged
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not represent a client, or where representation has commenced, shall withdraw from the representation of a client if the practitioner is discharged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing an application after a client has terminated the practitioner constitutes a violation of this rule. The decision finds the practitioner violated § 11.116(a)(3) by filing after being discharged.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.116(d) — protect client interests on termination
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon termination of representation, a practitioner shall take steps to the extent reasonably practicable to protect a client’s interests (reasonable notice, time to employ other counsel, surrendering papers/property, refunding unearned fees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations include knowingly filing an application after discharge, failing to deliver client papers or correct attorney signatures, and failing to refund unearned filing fees paid by the client.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1) — no false statement to a tribunal / correct false statements
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not knowingly make a false statement of fact or law to a tribunal or fail to correct a false statement of material fact or law previously made to the tribunal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: knowingly applying client signatures to power-of-attorney forms and filing them, filing applications after client termination, and otherwise submitting false facts to the Office. Practitioners must correct material falsities previously made.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(3) — not offer evidence known to be false; remedial measures
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not knowingly offer evidence that the practitioner knows to be false and, if material evidence offered is later known to be false, must take reasonable remedial measures, including disclosure to the tribunal if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying client signatures and filing known-false documents are given as conduct violating this rule; when falsity is discovered, the practitioner has an obligation to remediate.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b) — cooperate with OED investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not fail to cooperate with the Office of Enrollment and Discipline in an investigation, or knowingly fail to respond to a lawful demand or request for information from an admissions or disciplinary authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to respond to Requests for Information and Evidence (RFIs) sent under § 11.22(f), or to otherwise cooperate in investigations, constitutes a violation (example: the practitioner’s admitted nonresponse to the November 19, 2019 RFI).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c) — no conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative misconduct: filing applications after knowing client termination; applying client names as purported signatures; accepting payment and failing to remit filing fees or return funds; representing that fees would be submitted when they were not. The opinion notes that some neglect may be incompetence rather than intentional deceit, but finds other grounds supporting § 11.804(c) violations in this case.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d) — no conduct prejudicial to administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited include filing without authorization after termination and failing to respond to RFIs, which impede disciplinary and justice processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e) — consequence of failing to timely file an answer (default)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in entry of default judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Complaint warned that a decision by default may be entered if a written answer is not timely filed; the decision treats respondent’s failure to answer as admitting the allegations and forming the basis for findings of fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.35(b) — service by publication and answer deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: If a respondent cannot be confirmed to have received service, notice may be served by publication; the answer is due thirty days from the date of publication of the second notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The OED published two notices in the Official Gazette and set the respondent’s answer due 30 days after the second publication. The decision explains this procedural route and resulting deadline.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.11(a) — address-of-record service obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: A registered practitioner must notify the OED Director of the postal address for the practitioner’s office and provide written notice of any address change within 30 days of the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to maintain correct contact information may hinder service and disciplinary communications; the decision recounts attempted certified-mail service to respondent’s address of record and related problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.49 — burden and standard of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving any alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although respondent defaulted and admitted allegations, the decision reiterates that, generally, OED must meet the clear-and-convincing standard in disciplinary matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary purpose of legal discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary purpose of legal discipline is to protect the public and the administration of justice from practitioners who have not discharged, will not discharge, or are unlikely to properly discharge their professional duties, not to punish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle guides selection of sanctions (remedial/protective purpose). The decision cites precedent to explain sanctioning goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b) — four factors for determining sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining an appropriate sanction, the court must consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision applies these four factors to the admitted facts. Examples: breach of fiduciary duty to clients, intentional misconduct (applying signatures, not paying fees), substantial actual injury (abandoned applications), and multiple aggravators leading to exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factor — pattern of misconduct (STANDARDS § 9.22(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated or similar misconduct over time counts as an aggravating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision finds respondent had a pattern (prior 2017 warning involving false address and abandonment; similar 2018–2019 conduct). Pattern of misconduct supports a more severe sanction (exclusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factor — multiple offenses (STANDARDS § 9.22(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Commission of multiple offenses in a proceeding is an aggravating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Here the practitioner violated eleven separate provisions of the Rules; multiple rule violations weigh for harsher discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factor — refusal to acknowledge wrongdoing / lack of remorse (STANDARDS § 9.22(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner’s failure to acknowledge wrongful conduct or show remorse is an aggravating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent never apologized, returned funds, or otherwise acknowledged misconduct; lack of remorse supports a more severe sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factor — substantial experience in practice (STANDARDS § 9.22(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner’s substantial experience is an aggravating factor because a more experienced practitioner should know better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent had been registered since 2003 (~15 years); that experience is used to aggravate sanction severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factor — indifference to restitution (STANDARDS § 9.22(j))
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure or indifference to make restitution to harmed clients is an aggravating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent accepted funds for filing fees and failed to refund or remit them; the decision cites prior cases where failure to reimburse clients supported exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors (STANDARDS § 9.31) — potential reduction in discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigating factors, if shown, may justify reducing the degree of discipline imposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of mitigating considerations exist in the STANDARDS, but respondent did not participate and therefore presented no mitigating evidence; absence of mitigation is noted as a factor permitting harsher sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default admission equals findings of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: When a respondent defaults, the allegations in the Complaint are deemed admitted and may be set forth as the Court’s findings of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision treats respondent’s failure to answer as admitting the Complaint’s allegations and uses those admissions as the factual basis for rule violations and sanctioning analysis.
